[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Monolithic healthcare applications struggle with independent scaling, technology stack flexibility, deployment velocity, and team autonomy. Kubernetes orchestrates containerized applications but requires patterns for microservices communication, service discovery, resilience, and observability.
page_texts.5:
[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#solution-overview]

### Solution Overview

Implement microservices architecture pattern on Kubernetes with Deployment resources for stateless services, Service objects for service discovery, Ingress/ALB for external traffic, optional service mesh (Istio) for advanced traffic management, HorizontalPodAutoscaler for automatic scaling, and comprehensive health checks ensuring resilience.
page_texts.6:
[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#when-to-use]

### When to Use

- Large healthcare applications benefiting from service decomposition
- Teams requiring independent deployment and scaling of components
- Applications with varying resource requirements across services
- Systems requiring polyglot language support (.NET, Python, Node.js)
page_texts.7:
[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#benefits]

### Benefits

- **Independent Scaling**: Scale services based on individual demand
- **Technology Flexibility**: Services use optimal language/framework
- **Deployment Velocity**: Deploy services independently without coordinating releases
- **Team Autonomy**: Teams own services end-to-end
- **Resilience**: Service failures isolated, circuit breakers prevent cascading failures

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#target-audience]

## Target Audience

This pattern is intended for:

- **Platform Engineer**: Configures Kubernetes Deployment, Service, Ingress, and HPA resources for microservices workloads.
- **Application Architect**: Designs service decomposition, API contracts, and resilience patterns for microservices architectures.
- **DevOps Engineer**: Implements CI/CD pipelines, GitOps workflows, and deployment strategies for independent microservice releases.
- **Site Reliability Engineer**: Monitors service health, configures distributed tracing, and manages service mesh configurations.

page_texts.12:
[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#problem-details]

### Problem Details

**Monolithic Challenges:**
- Single deployment unit (entire app redeployed for minor changes)
- Scaling entire application even when only one component overloaded
- Technology lock-in (entire app in one language/framework)
- Team coordination overhead (merge conflicts, deploy scheduling)
- Single point of failure (app crash affects all functionality)

**Microservices Requirements:**
- Service-to-service communication (REST, gRPC, messaging)
- Dynamic service discovery
- Load balancing and traffic management
- Resilience (retries, timeouts, circuit breakers)
- Distributed tracing and observability

### Forces and Constraints

_Balance microservices benefits with operational complexity, network latency of inter-service calls, eventual consistency challenges, distributed transaction coordination, testing complexity._

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#pattern-description]

### Pattern Description

**Microservices on Kubernetes Architecture:**

**Core Components:**
1. **Deployment**: Stateless microservice with replica sets, rolling updates
2. **Service**: Stable ClusterIP for service discovery
3. **Ingress/ALB**: External traffic routing to services
4. **HorizontalPodAutoscaler**: Auto-scale based on CPU/memory/custom metrics
5. **ConfigMap/Secret**: Environment-specific configuration
6. **Health Checks**: Liveness and readiness probes

**Optional Enhancements:**
- **Service Mesh (Istio)**: mTLS, traffic management, observability
- **API Gateway (Kong, Ambassador)**: Authentication, rate limiting, aggregation
- **Messaging (Kafka, SQS)**: Asynchronous communication
- **Distributed Tracing (X-Ray, Jaeger)**: Request flow visualization
page_texts.16:
[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#architecture-diagram]

### Architecture Diagram

```text
Microservices Architecture
===========================

[ AWS ALB: API Gateway ]
       ↓
[ Ingress Controller ]
       ↓ routes
[ Kubernetes Services: ClusterIP ]
       ↓ load balances
[ Microservice Pods ]
       ↓ communicates
[ Service-to-Service: Internal APIs ]
       ↓ persists
[ Databases: StatefulSets/External ]

Optional Service Mesh (Istio):

- Sidecar Proxies: Envoy
- Traffic Management: Canary, Circuit Breaker
- Observability: Distributed Tracing
- Security: mTLS
```

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#components]

### Components

| Component | Responsibility | Dependencies |
|-----------|----------------|--------------|
| **Deployment** | Manage replica sets, rolling updates, rollback | Container image, resource limits |
| **Service** | Stable networking endpoint, load balancing across pods | Pod selector labels |
| **Ingress/ALB** | HTTP(S) routing, TLS termination | AWS Load Balancer Controller |
| **HPA** | Automatic horizontal scaling based on metrics | Metrics Server |
| **Service Mesh** | mTLS, traffic splitting, circuit breaking | Istio control plane |
| **API Gateway** | Authentication, rate limiting, request routing | Kong or Ambassador |

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#configuration-examples]

### Configuration Examples

```yaml
# Deployment: Stateless Web Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: claims-service
  namespace: production
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: claims-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: claims-service
        version: v1
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: claims-service-sa

      # Pod-level security context (recommended: GUID-SEC-APPS-KUBERNETES-PLATFORM-2.7.04)
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10000
        fsGroup: 10000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault

      containers:
      - name: claims-service
        image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/claims-service:v1.2.3

        # Container-level security context (recommended: Pod Security Standards - Restricted)
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 10000
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          protocol: TCP

        # Writable temp directory (required for readOnlyRootFilesystem)
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
        - name: cache
          mountPath: /app/cache

        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
          limits:
            memory: "1Gi"
            cpu: "1000m"

        # Health checks (required for zero-downtime deployments)
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5

        env:
        - name: DATABASE_HOST
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: claims-config
              key: database.host

        # Secret from External Secrets Operator (recommended: PTN-SEC-SECRETS-001)
        # This secret is synced from AWS Secrets Manager
        - name: DATABASE_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: claims-secret-external  # Created by ExternalSecret CRD
              key: database.password

      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: cache
        emptyDir: {}

---
# Service
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: claims-service
  namespace: production
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: claims-service
  ports:

  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
    protocol: TCP

---
# HorizontalPodAutoscaler
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: claims-service-hpa
  namespace: production
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: claims-service
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:

  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70

  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80

---
# NetworkPolicy (recommended: PTN-SEC-K8S-004 for zero-trust architecture)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: claims-service-netpol
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: claims-service
  policyTypes:

  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  # Allow traffic from ingress controller
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: ingress-nginx
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
  egress:
  # Allow database access
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
  # Allow DNS resolution
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
  # Allow HTTPS to external APIs (AWS services, etc.)
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
```

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#security-configuration-explained]

### Security Configuration Explained

The configuration above follows organizational security recommendations:

**Pod Security Standards (Restricted):**
- `runAsNonRoot: true` - Prevents container from running as root user (UID 0)
- `runAsUser: 10000` - Explicitly sets non-root user ID
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` - Blocks privilege escalation attacks via setuid binaries
- `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` - Removes all Linux capabilities, minimizing kernel attack surface
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` - Enforces immutable container filesystem preventing malware persistence
- `seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault` - Applies default seccomp profile restricting system calls

**Rationale**: These controls are recommended by GUID-SEC-APPS-KUBERNETES-PLATFORM-2.7.04 --> --> §2.1 to prevent container escape and privilege escalation attacks. The `emptyDir` volumes provide writable directories (`/tmp`, `/app/cache`) when applications require temporary file storage.

**External Secrets Management:**
The example references `claims-secret-external` created by External Secrets Operator ([PTN-SEC-K8S-003](../../security/kubernetes/PTN-SEC-K8S-003-security-secrets-management-pattern.md)). This is recommended over native Kubernetes Secrets for:

- Encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS keys
- Automated rotation without pod restarts
- Centralized audit trail via CloudTrail
- Compliance with HIPAA encryption requirements (§164.312(a)(2)(iv))

**Network Policies (Zero-Trust):**
Default-deny NetworkPolicy with explicit allow rules ([PTN-SEC-K8S-004](../../security/kubernetes/PTN-SEC-K8S-004-security-zero-trust-pattern.md)) prevents lateral movement if pod is compromised. This implements micro-segmentation required for:

- HIPAA PHI workloads (§164.312(a)(1) - Access Control)
- Zero-trust architecture principles ("never trust, always verify")
- Blast radius reduction in multi-tenant clusters

**Container Image Security:**
Production deployments must use container images following GUID-SEC-APPS-CONTAINER-SECURITY-2.7.05 --> -->:

- Distroless or minimal base images (Alpine, AWS minimal)
- Multi-stage builds removing build tools from production images
- Image signing with Cosign for supply chain integrity
- SBOM generation for vulnerability tracking
- Base image pinning with SHA256 digests (not mutable tags)
- Non-root user created in Dockerfile

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#best-practices]

### Best Practices

- Design services around business capabilities
- API-first development with OpenAPI specifications
- Implement comprehensive health checks (liveness, readiness)
- Configure appropriate resource limits to prevent resource exhaustion
- Use circuit breakers for external dependencies
- Implement distributed tracing from day one
- Graceful shutdown for zero-downtime deployments
- Versioned APIs for backward compatibility
- Follow Pod Security Standards (Restricted) for all production workloads
- Use External Secrets Operator for all sensitive credentials
- Implement NetworkPolicies for defense-in-depth security

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

- Overly granular microservices ("nanoservices")
- Insufficient monitoring and observability
- Missing circuit breakers causing cascading failures
- Inadequate resource limits leading to OOM kills
- Tight coupling between services
- Distributed transactions without compensation logic
- Missing health checks causing traffic to unhealthy pods

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#compliance-requirements]

### Compliance Requirements

**Security Controls (Recommended):**
- Pod Security Standards (Restricted) enforcement via admission controller
- External secrets management (AWS Secrets Manager via External Secrets Operator)
- NetworkPolicies implementing default-deny with explicit allow rules
- Container images signed with Cosign and verified at deployment
- SBOM generation for all production images
- Non-root containers with read-only root filesystem
- Resource limits preventing denial-of-service attacks

**Application Standards:**
- Services must implement health check endpoints (liveness, readiness)
- API contracts documented via OpenAPI specifications
- Distributed tracing instrumentation required

**HIPAA Requirements (for PHI workloads):**
- Encryption at rest (KMS-encrypted secrets, encrypted EBS volumes)
- Encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+ for all external traffic)
- Comprehensive audit logging (application logs to CloudWatch)
- Network isolation via NetworkPolicies
- See [PTN-SEC-K8S-001](../../security/kubernetes/PTN-SEC-K8S-001-security-hipaa-compliance-pattern.md) for complete requirements

### Real-World Example 1: Claims Processing Decomposition

**Context**: Monolithic claims processing system handling high-volume annual encounters with lengthy deployment windows

**Implementation**:
1. Identified bounded contexts: Claims Submission, Claims Adjudication, Payment Processing, Reporting, Member Portal
2. Extracted Claims Submission first using strangler fig pattern (API Gateway routing 10% traffic to new service)
3. Each service deployed as separate Deployment with dedicated Service
4. Claims Submission scaled independently (3-15 replicas based on submission volume)
5. Claims Adjudication with GPU-enabled nodes for ML-based fraud detection (Python)
6. Payment Processing in .NET Core with strict HIPAA compliance controls
7. Reporting service with read replicas scaling to 20+ replicas during month-end

**Technologies**:
- Claims Submission: Node.js with Express
- Claims Adjudication: Python with TensorFlow for ML models
- Payment Processing: .NET Core
- Reporting: Python with Pandas/NumPy
- Member Portal: React frontend with Node.js BFF

**Outcome**:
- Deployment time reduced from 45 minutes to 8 minutes per service
- Claims Submission scaling independently during enrollment periods (3x load)
- 99.97% uptime achieved with isolated failure domains
- Teams deploying 4x more frequently (weekly vs. monthly)

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#real-world-example-2-istio-service-mesh-for-advanced-traffic-management]

### Real-World Example 2: Istio Service Mesh for Advanced Traffic Management

**Context**: Microservices architecture requiring canary deployments, circuit breakers, mutual TLS

**Implementation**:
1. Installed Istio control plane (istiod) in dedicated namespace
2. Enabled sidecar injection via namespace label: `istio-injection=enabled`
3. Configured VirtualService for canary deployment (90% v1, 10% v2)
4. DestinationRule with circuit breaker: max connections 100, max pending requests 1000
5. PeerAuthentication enforcing mutual TLS (STRICT mode)
6. AuthorizationPolicy limiting Claims Adjudication service to only receive traffic from Claims Submission
7. Kiali dashboard for service mesh observability

**Canary Deployment Example**:
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: claims-service
spec:
  hosts:

  - claims-service
  http:

  - match:
    - headers:
        x-test-user:
          exact: "true"
    route:
    - destination:
        host: claims-service
        subset: v2

  - route:
    - destination:
        host: claims-service
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: claims-service
        subset: v2
      weight: 10
```

**Outcome**:
- Zero-downtime deployments with automated canary analysis
- Circuit breakers prevented cascading failures (1 incident avoided)
- Mutual TLS enforced with no application code changes
- P95 latency reduced 15% with connection pooling

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#real-world-example-3-api-gateway-with-aws-alb]

### Real-World Example 3: API Gateway with AWS ALB

**Context**: External client access requiring authentication, rate limiting, request routing

**Implementation**:
1. AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) as API Gateway
2. ALB Ingress Controller managing ALB via Ingress resources
3. Path-based routing: `/api/claims` → claims-service, `/api/members` → member-service
4. AWS WAF attached to ALB for rate limiting (1000 req/min per IP)
5. AWS Cognito integration for OAuth2 authentication
6. OIDC authentication via ALB rules (redirecting to Cognito)
7. Backend services receive `X-Amzn-OIDC-Data` header with user identity

**Ingress Configuration**:
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:...
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-policy: ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS-1-2-2017-01
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-type: cognito
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/auth-idp-cognito: '{"userPoolArn":"arn:aws:cognito-idp:...","userPoolClientId":"..."}'
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:

  - host: api.gainwell-medicaid.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api/claims
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: claims-service
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /api/members
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: member-service
            port:
              number: 80
```

**Outcome**:
- Single entry point with centralized authentication
- Rate limiting preventing DDoS (blocked 15K malicious requests in Q1)
- SSL termination at ALB reducing backend compute
- Path-based routing enabling service discoverability

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#scenario-1-independent-scaling-during-month-end-reporting]

#### Scenario 1: Independent Scaling During Month-End Reporting

1. Month-end triggers reporting workload (500% increase in traffic)
2. Reporting service HorizontalPodAutoscaler detects CPU >70%
3. HPA scales Reporting service from 3 to 18 replicas over 5 minutes
4. Claims Submission, Adjudication services remain at baseline (3 replicas)
5. After reporting completes, HPA scales down to baseline within 10 minutes
6. Cost optimized: Only scale services under load

**Metrics**:
- Reporting service: 3 → 18 replicas (6x scaling)
- Claims services: 3 replicas (unchanged)
- Cost optimized: only services under load scaled, not the entire monolith

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#scenario-2-technology-flexibility-for-ml-fraud-detection]

#### Scenario 2: Technology Flexibility for ML Fraud Detection

1. Claims Adjudication service requires ML model for fraud detection
2. Original .NET service cannot efficiently run TensorFlow models
3. Extract Fraud Detection as separate Python microservice
4. Python service deployed with GPU-enabled nodes (p3.2xlarge)
5. Claims Adjudication calls Fraud Detection via REST API
6. Fraud Detection scales independently (GPU nodes expensive, only scale when needed)

**Technologies**:
- Claims Adjudication: .NET Core (business logic)
- Fraud Detection: Python + TensorFlow + FastAPI (ML inference)
- Communication: Synchronous REST with circuit breaker (timeout 2s)

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#scenario-3-zero-downtime-deployment-with-canary]

#### Scenario 3: Zero-Downtime Deployment with Canary

1. New version of Claims Submission service (v2) ready for deployment
2. Deploy v2 Deployment alongside v1 (both running)
3. Istio VirtualService routes 10% traffic to v2, 90% to v1
4. Monitor error rate, latency for 30 minutes
5. If metrics healthy, gradually increase v2 traffic (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%)
6. If metrics degrade, revert to 100% v1 traffic immediately
7. Once v2 at 100%, delete v1 Deployment

**Automated Canary Analysis (Flagger)**:
```yaml
apiVersion: flagger.app/v1beta1
kind: Canary
metadata:
  name: claims-service
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: claims-service
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600
  service:
    port: 80
  analysis:
    interval: 1m
    threshold: 5
    maxWeight: 50
    stepWeight: 10
    metrics:
    - name: request-success-rate
      thresholdRange:
        min: 99
      interval: 1m
    - name: request-duration
      thresholdRange:
        max: 500
      interval: 1m
```

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#scenario-4-circuit-breaker-preventing-cascading-failure]

#### Scenario 4: Circuit Breaker Preventing Cascading Failure

1. Payment Processing service experiencing database overload (response time >5s)
2. Claims Adjudication calls Payment Processing synchronously
3. Without circuit breaker: Claims Adjudication threads blocked waiting for Payment Processing, eventually exhausting thread pool
4. With circuit breaker (Istio DestinationRule):
   - After 5 consecutive errors, circuit opens
   - Subsequent requests fail fast (immediate 503 response)
   - Circuit half-opens after 30s to test recovery
   - If successful, circuit closes; otherwise, remains open
5. Claims Adjudication continues processing claims, queues payments for later

**Outcome**: Payment Processing incident isolated, Claims Adjudication maintained 99.9% uptime

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#before-monolithic-architecture]

#### Before (Monolithic Architecture)

**Deployment**:
- Entire application deployed as single artifact (30-45 minute deployment)
- All-or-nothing deployment (rollback requires full application rollback)
- Monthly deployment cadence due to risk and coordination overhead
- Zero-downtime deployment impossible (rolling restart required)

**Scaling**:
- Entire application scales together (even if only reporting under load)
- Manual scaling (ops team updates replica count)
- Over-provisioned to handle peak load (80% idle capacity during off-peak)

**Technology**:
- Single technology stack (.NET Framework 4.8)
- Cannot leverage Python for ML, Node.js for async I/O
- Shared dependencies causing version conflicts

**Resilience**:
- Single failure point (entire app down if any component fails)
- Database connection exhaustion affects all features
- No circuit breakers (cascading failures common)

**Team Organization**:
- Cross-functional team managing entire application
- Merge conflicts common (50+ developers in single codebase)
- Long feature branch lifetimes (2-4 weeks)
page_texts.46:
[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#after-microservices-on-kubernetes]

#### After (Microservices on Kubernetes)

**Deployment**:
- Services deployed independently (5-10 minute deployment per service)
- Canary deployments with automated rollback (error rate >1%)
- Weekly+ deployment cadence per service (some teams deploying daily)
- Zero-downtime deployments standard (rolling updates with readiness probes)

**Scaling**:
- Services scale independently based on demand (HPA with CPU/memory metrics)
- Automatic scaling (HPA scales within 30 seconds of threshold breach)
- Right-sized resources (60-70% utilization during normal operations)
- Cost savings: 35% reduction vs. monolithic over-provisioning

**Technology**:
- Polyglot architecture:
  - Claims Submission: Node.js (async I/O for high throughput)
  - Claims Adjudication: .NET Core (business logic)
  - Fraud Detection: Python + TensorFlow (ML)
  - Reporting: Python + Pandas (data processing)
- Each service uses optimal technology for requirements

**Resilience**:
- Isolated failure domains (Claims Submission failure doesn't affect Member Portal)
- Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures (Istio DestinationRule)
- Connection pooling per service (database connection exhaustion isolated)
- 99.97% uptime vs. 99.7% with monolith (70% reduction in downtime)

**Team Organization**:
- Service teams with full ownership (dev, test, deploy, monitor)
- Reduced merge conflicts (teams work in separate repositories)
- Short-lived feature branches (1-3 days, continuous integration)
- 4x increase in deployment frequency

[patterns/application/kubernetes/PTN-APP-K8S-003-application-microservices-architecture-pattern.md#tldr]

## TL;DR

**Problem:** Monolithic applications cannot scale components independently, lack technology flexibility, have slow deployment velocity (30-45 min), single failure domain causing cascading failures.

**Solution:** Microservices architecture on Kubernetes with Deployment resources, Service objects for discovery, HorizontalPodAutoscaler for automatic scaling, health checks (liveness/readiness), optional Istio service mesh for advanced traffic management (canary deployments, circuit breakers, mutual TLS).

**When to Use:** Large applications benefiting from decomposition (>5 services), varying resource requirements per service, independent team development, polyglot technology requirements, high deployment frequency needs (weekly+).

**Key Benefits:**
- Independent scaling per service (3-20 replicas based on demand)
- Technology flexibility (Node.js, .NET Core, Python per service requirements)
- Faster deployment velocity (5-10 min vs. 45 min)
- Team autonomy with full ownership
- Isolated failure domains (99.97% uptime vs. 99.7% monolith)
- 35% cost reduction via right-sizing resources

**Implementation Complexity:** Medium-High - Requires service decomposition strategy, API contract design, distributed tracing, service mesh setup (optional)

**Prerequisites:** Containerized services, defined service boundaries (Domain-Driven Design), API contracts (OpenAPI), Kubernetes expertise, distributed tracing instrumentation

**Related Patterns:** Event-Driven Processing, Batch Processing, GitOps Deployment, Unified Observability, Network Architecture
